battle.title: Array Traversal Trial
battle.description: Walk the arrays without falling off the end.

questions.text: For  int[] a = new int[5];  which index is the LAST valid one?
questions.explanation: Indexes run from 0 to length - 1, so a 5-element array ends at a[4]. a[5] is the classic off-by-one and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
The loop steps by 2 starting at index 0, so it visits indexes 0, 2 and 4: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12. Adding every element would give 14, and starting at index 1 would visit indexes 1 and 3 for just 1 + 1 = 2.
The reverse loop condition is i > 0, so it stops before index 0 and never prints 1. To include the first element it must be i >= 0.

questions.text: You must double every element of an int array in place. Which traversal works?
options: Enhanced for loop assigning to the loop variable
Enhanced for loop followed by a.length++
Clone the array and double only the copy
Indexed for loop assigning to a[i]
questions.answer: Indexed for loop assigning to a[i]
questions.explanation: The enhanced for variable is only a copy of each element, so assigning to it never changes the array. Writing through the index changes the real element.
In an enhanced for loop x is a copy of each primitive element, so x *= 10 changes only the copy. The array stays {2, 4, 6} and the sum is 12, not 120.

debug.title: The Missing Maximum
debug.description: The program reads n integers and should print the largest one. It works on some inputs but prints a wrong answer on others. Input: n, then n integers (they may be negative). Output: the maximum.
hints: Try the input '3' then '-5 -2 -9'. What should the maximum be?
Everything in the loop looks fine. Look at the value max has before the loop starts.
Starting at 0 means a number can only win if it beats 0. What if every number is negative?
Start max at the first element, int max = a[0], so it always begins as a real array value.
